Subject: Dedicated commit & spike settlement — clarification

Hi Dylan,

Thanks for the product overview last week. We're finalizing sizing for a dedicated GPU pool and Procurement has a couple of questions about how you handle above-commit usage. Two specific asks:

1) If our traffic briefly spikes above the committed pool (e.g., 2–3x baseline for 1–5 minutes), will we be throttled or billed? How does Redwood differentiate short bursts vs sustained overage?

2) How do you meter Dedicated usage — per GPU-hour, per second of GPU runtime, or by generated tokens/throughput? We need a sample invoice calc for a realistic monthly profile (baseline + 5 spikes).

Also attaching our RFP excerpt for context (Acme_RFP_Dedicated_Requirements.pdf). Procurement is sensitive to surprise overage charges — they prefer a predictable cap or pre-purchased buffer. Can you provide the commercial options and any standard amendment language?

Best,

From: Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.ai>

Hi Jared — thanks for the clear asks and for sharing the RFP. High-level options we offer for Dedicated overage handling (summary + example attached):

1) Soft-burst buffer (recommended for latency-sensitive workloads)
   - You get a committed pool (GPU-hours/week). We provide a small monthly buffer (e.g., 10% of commit) for free to absorb short spikes.
   - After buffer is consumed, short bursts (under 2 minutes) are permitted at discounted overage rates; sustained usage triggers request-level throttling to preserve cluster stability.

2) Step-priced overage (pay-as-you-go)
   - Overage metered and billed at defined tiers: 0–20% over commit = X/unit, 20–50% = Y/unit, >50% = Z/unit. No automatic throttling until a sustained 60-minute threshold.

3) Pre-purchased burst credits
   - You buy a block of burst GPU-hours at a discounted rate (e.g., 30% off). Credits are consumed for above-commit usage before step-pricing applies.

Metering: we meter Dedicated at the GPU-second level aggregated into 60s windows and convert to GPU-hour equivalents for billing. That means a 30-second spike on one GPU will bill as 30 GPU-seconds; we round to the nearest minute for reporting.

Example (attached): baseline commit = 10 GPU-hours/day, 5 short spikes of 3 minutes each across the month. We included three commercial permutations (soft-burst, step-priced, burst credits) so you can compare month-end invoices.

I've looped Marcus for the technical metering details and Grace for the billing/commercial language. Attached: redwood_dedicated_overage_options_v1.pdf.

If you can tell us which of the three approaches you prefer, we will produce a redline-ready amendment and an invoice preview for your procurement team.

Cheers,
Dylan Brooks
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Hi Jared — adding a technical view so Procurement has a clear picture of behavior at the request layer and how metering maps to your traffic patterns.

Metering and enforcement details (short version):
- Recording: we sample GPU utilization at 1s granularity and aggregate to 60s windows for billing. Billing aligns to GPU-seconds -> GPU-hours. Reports show per-route and per-model breakdowns.
- Burst handling: we distinguish burst vs sustained by two parameters: magnitude (x-times baseline) and duration. Default thresholds: >5x baseline for <= 120s is classified as a short burst; >120s or >3x baseline sustained beyond 60 minutes is candidate for throttling.
- Throttling semantics: when a pool is exhausted under enforced policy, we return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header; we also provide a grace-failure bucket (configurable) that can absorb N requests before 429s start.
- Failover: we can optionally route excess traffic to a compatible smaller model variant (e.g., 7B quantized) to preserve success rates at degraded latency/quality.

Notes on caching and KV: prefix and KV cache reduce downstream GPU time for repeated conversational context — meter reflects actual GPU execution only.

Attached is a one-sheet (metering_spec_sheet.xlsx) with sample metrics and an example rule config you could request in the amendment. Happy to run your sample trace file against our model to produce a month-end estimate.

—Marcus
Sr Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Dedicated commit & spike settlement — updated commercial proposal

Jared — appreciate the clarity. We discussed internally (sales + finance + solutions) and here's a pragmatic counter that balances predictability for Acme with platform stewardship:

Commercial counter-offer (summary):
- 12-month committed Dedicated pool: 12% discount on committed capacity (we can stretch to 15% for a 24-month term).
- Pre-purchased burst credits: 30% discount off list for a minimum purchase of 100 GPU-hours.
- Soft-burst forgiveness: first 10% of overage (monthly) is waived for standard customers; for Acme we can extend to 15% waived if you commit to a 12-month term and purchase the minimum burst credits.
- Step-pricing thereafter: 0–25% over = burst credit consumption (discounted); 25–75% over = +25% premium to list burst rate; >75% = full overage rate + possible throttling after sustained 60 minutes.

Throttling/SLA credit clause (proposal):
- Measurement: client-visible 429 errors attributable to Dedicated pool enforcement are measured at the route level in 1-minute windows and aggregated daily.
- Credit trigger: if client-visible 429s attributable to enforcement exceed 3% of total successful requests in a 30-day rolling window, Redwood will issue a service credit equal to 5% of the monthly invoice for the impacted month.
- Cap: credits capped at 50% of the monthly invoice. Credits are applied to subsequent invoices and are not cash refunds.
- Exclusions: credits won't apply for customer misconfiguration, scheduled maintenance (with >48h notice), or spikes clearly outside the contracted buffering policy (e.g., DDoS).

Attached: commercial_summary_v3.pdf (with sample invoice calc using your expected profile). We also included a DocuSign-ready amendment link to accept this option.

If that looks acceptable, Grace can draft the amendment and we can route to legal for a quick redline.

Best,
Dylan Brooks
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
